A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DFT research, with matching authors, method, and original experiments. Text, equations, tables, and figures support reliable comparison. v1 has no separate appendix; v2's Appendix A contains readable new and relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original mathematical-reasoning experiments, offline/online RL comparisons, training curves, token-distribution analysis, and hyperparameter sweeps.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds code-generation, multimodal-reasoning, OpenR1-training, and LoRA experiments.

M1.justification: The final token-level DFT objective in Equation 9 is unchanged: detached target-token probabilities weight the negative log-likelihood. The offline rejection-sampling approach is retained. The new domains and LoRA experiments apply this existing objective without introducing a new proposed algorithm component.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates text-based mathematical reasoning. v2 adds UltraFeedback training and code evaluation on HumanEval, HumanEval+, and eight-language MultiPL-E, plus WeThink training and visual mathematical reasoning on MathVerse, MathVision, and WeMath. Appendix A.6 also evaluates training with OpenR1 reasoning traces.

E2.justification: The ordinary SFT reference in v1 Table 3, with average accuracy 16.81, disappears from the corresponding offline-setting comparisons. DPO, RFT, PPO, and GRPO remain. The iw-SFT comparisons are retained in v2 Tables 5–6, rather than removed; the new domains reuse base-model and SFT comparators.

E3.justification: Section 4.2.1 revises the reported rejection-sampling pool from 10,000 to 100,000 questions, retaining four responses per question and approximately 140,000 accepted examples; this does not establish that experiments were rerun. New protocols include code training with batch size 16, one-epoch multimodal training, three-epoch OpenR1 training, and LoRA with rank 8 and alpha 16.

E4.justification: Appendices A.6–A.7 add limited checks of whether DFT's advantage persists with alternative, higher-quality reasoning supervision and parameter-efficient LoRA training. The token-distribution investigation and learning-rate/batch-size sweeps are retained. Moving the latter to Appendix A.8 does not constitute a new ablation.

E5.justification: Both versions report mathematical accuracy averaged over 16 decoding runs. Neither reports training-seed variability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new result tables introduce no additional uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Tables 3–4 and 7–8. Examples include Qwen2.5-Coder-7B HumanEval scores of 67.7 for DFT versus 54.9 for SFT, and Qwen2.5-VL-3B MathVerse overall scores of 37.54 versus 35.66. Original mathematical table values are retained apart from the removed SFT row averaging 16.81; the relocated iw-SFT results and all three plots are unchanged.

T1.justification: Appendix A.4 adds an explicit derivation showing that the per-example detached-probability-weighted loss has gradient -∇π, contrasting it with cross-entropy's -(1/π)∇π. Appendix A.3 expands the existing importance-sampling identity rather than establishing a new theorem. The final method remains unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction explicitly extend the generalization claim to code generation and multimodal reasoning. The central SFT/RL equivalence, probability reweighting, and offline-RL contributions remain. The introduction also replaces its explicit unbounded-variance assertion with excessive-gradient and unstable-optimization language.

C2.justification: Appendix A.4 adds a noisy-demonstration interpretation of confidence weighting and discusses stability, calibration, and preservation of the pretraining distribution. Appendix A.2 newly qualifies that conventional SFT may remain preferable for factual-knowledge acquisition. These extend the existing overfitting interpretation; they are not new empirical demonstrations of noise robustness.

D1.justification: v2 documents UltraFeedback response selection and training settings, LLaMA-Factory/VLMEvalKit for multimodal experiments, OpenR1 filtering and training epochs, and LoRA parameters. It also newly identifies the official Qwen2.5-Math evaluation pipeline for the retained math experiments, without establishing a pipeline change. The promised code release remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds comparisons with MixCE and GOLD, while Appendix A.4 connects DFT to robust boosting and learning from noisy demonstrations. References also expand for the new datasets and tools. These refine the existing SFT–RL positioning rather than replace it; the explicit 'first to' formulation is removed.

P1.justification: The introduction and related work undergo extensive rewriting and condensation, and experimental setup paragraphs are reorganized. The experimental narrative now separates mathematical reasoning, offline RL, code generation, multimodal reasoning, and analysis. Existing iw-SFT discussion, limitations, and hyperparameter analysis move into a structured appendix alongside new explanations.

P2.justification: Four new tables display code, multimodal, OpenR1, and LoRA results. v1 Table 3 is reorganized across v2 Tables 2 and 6, while the original iw-SFT table moves to Appendix A.5 as Table 5. Figure 3 moves to the appendix. All three underlying plots are retained, with limited caption edits.

improvement.justification: v2 directly addresses v1's stated math-only, text-only validation limitation through code-generation and visual-math comparisons against SFT (Tables 3–4). OpenR1 and LoRA checks further support applicability, while the appendix clarifies gradient scaling and adds a meaningful factual-learning caveat. Some reporting errors remain, including Appendix A.7 confusing LLaMA's base and SFT scores, but the new comparisons substantially strengthen evidence for the central generalization claim.
